title: Truthiness of 0
explanation: Only nil and false are falsy in Ruby. 0, "" and [] are all truthy, unlike Python or JavaScript.

title: Array.new with a default object
explanation: Array.new(3, []) puts the same array object in every slot, so appending to one shows up in all three. Use Array.new(3) { [] } to get a fresh array per slot.

title: Hash.new with a default array
explanation: h[:a] returns the shared default array without storing it under :a, so << mutates the default and the hash stays empty (h[:b] is now [1]). Use Hash.new { |hash, k| hash[k] = [] }.

title: Symbol and string keys
explanation: "name" and :name are different keys. Hash#[] returns nil for a missing key; Hash#fetch would raise KeyError.

title: ||= on false
code:
enabled = false
enabled ||= true
p enabled
explanation: a ||= b assigns when a is falsy, and false is falsy. That makes ||= the wrong tool for defaulting a boolean that may legitimately be false.

title: return inside a block
code:
def find_big
  [1, 2, 3].each { |x| return x * 10 if x == 2 }
  :none
end
p find_big
explanation: return in a block returns from the method the block was written in, so find_big returns 20 at once. (In a lambda, return only leaves the lambda.)

title: << mutates a shared string
code:
a = "hi"
b = a
b << "!"
p a
explanation: a and b refer to the same String, and << appends in place. b += "!" would build a new string and leave a as "hi".

title: Integer division
explanation: Dividing two Integers gives an Integer, rounded toward negative infinity. Make one side a Float (7 / 2.0 or 7.fdiv(2)) to get 3.5.
